title: Data Exploration and Visualisation
text:
This page presents the main visual patterns found in the MC1 communication data. The purpose is to show how the embargo breach developed over time, how communication behaviour changed, and what warning signs appeared before the early release.
The visual exploration focuses on five areas:

stock and external pressure;
communication volume;
side-channel activity;
public signalling; and
leading indicators before the release.


1 Setup and Loading Prepared Data
Firstly, we will load the R packages and data prepared.

pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse, lubridate, ggrepel, knitr, DT, scales
)

rounds_tbl        <- readr::read_rds("../data/rds/rounds.rds")
comms_tbl         <- readr::read_rds("../data/rds/communications.rds")
participants_tbl  <- readr::read_rds("../data/rds/participants.rds")
edges_weighted    <- readr::read_rds("../data/rds/network_edges.rds")

stock_tbl <- rounds_tbl |>
  select(round_index, hour, stock_price_clean, is_corrupt, market_sentiment)



2 Crisis Timeline and Stock Pressure
The first view shows the external pressure on TenantThread. The stock price decline helps explain why the agents became more urgent and aggressive in managing the release.


Code
stock_tbl %>%
  filter(!is.na(stock_price_clean)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = stock_price_clean)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#1a587a") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(data = events, aes(xintercept = hour), linetype = "dashed") +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = events,
    aes(x = hour, y = max(stock_tbl$stock_price_clean, na.rm = TRUE), label = label),
    size = 3.2,
    direction = "x",
    min.segment.length = 0
  ) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "3 days") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "$TTHR stock price and key crisis events",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Stock price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









The chart shows that $TTHR’s stock price was already declining before the embargo breach. This does not prove the release decision by itself, but it provides important context: the agents were operating under growing market and reputational pressure before the early release occurred.


3 Communication Volume Over Time
This chart shows how communication intensity changed across the timeline.


Code
msg_daily <- comms_tbl %>%
  mutate(day = as_date(round_hour)) %>%
  count(day, channel_type)

ggplot(msg_daily, aes(x = day, y = n, fill = channel_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.3, size = 3.2) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = as.numeric(ymd("2046-06-05")),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#a7661c"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ channel_type, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Internal" = "#1a587a",
      "Public" = "#458ab0"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "2 days") +
  labs(
    title = "Daily message volume by channel type",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of messages"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )









The chart shows a sharp increase in message volume on Jun 5, the day of the embargo breach. Internal messages increased the most, showing intense crisis coordination. Public posts also increased, suggesting the issue had already moved beyond private channels before the final release.


4 Side-channel Use vs Main Channel
This chart compares the main communication huddle against side channels and public posts. It is important because side channels reduce visibility and make the system harder to control.


Code
comms_tbl %>%
  mutate(
    day = as_date(round_hour),
    channel_group = case_when(
      channel == "comms_huddle" ~ "Main huddle",
      channel %in% c("side_huddle", "one_on_one_chat") ~ "Side / 1-to-1",
      is_public ~ "Public posts",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(channel_group)) %>%
  count(day, channel_group) %>%
  ggplot(aes(day, n, colour = channel_group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(ymd("2046-06-05")),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "#a7661c") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "2 days") +
  labs(
    title = "Side-channel use before the breach",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Messages per day",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )









The chart shows that side-channels were already active before the Jun 5 breach. This is meaningful because they are less visible than the main huddle, making it harder to monitor release-related coordination. Public posts also appeared around the breach, showing that the crisis had already spread beyond internal channels.

text:
1.2 Stock Price Trajectory and Pressure Context
The stock decline is the external pressure that motivated increasingly aggressive attempts to break the embargo early.


Code
stock_plot <- stock_tbl |> filter(!is.na(stock_price_clean))

# Key annotated events — each sourced from environment_context or comms_tbl
events <- tribble(
  ~hour,                           ~label,
  ymd_hms("2046-05-22T09:00:00"), "NHPI report (R4)",
  ymd_hms("2046-05-29T09:00:00"), "@Elena faux pas (R9)",
  ymd_hms("2046-06-04T09:00:00"), "SaltWind exposé (R13)",
  ymd_hms("2046-06-05T17:17:00"), "Breach ~17:17 (R22)"
)

ggplot(stock_plot, aes(x = hour, y = stock_price_clean)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(data = events, aes(xintercept = hour), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_text(data = events, aes(x = hour, y = 39, label = label),
            size = 2.8, hjust = 0, nudge_x = 3600 * 5) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "3 days") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format()) +

title: Analysis
text:
1.3 Message Volume Over Time
How did communication volume and channel use shift across the crisis?


Code
comms_tbl |>
  count(round_hour, channel_type) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = round_hour, y = n, fill = channel_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 3600 * 4) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "4 days") +
  labs(
    title = "Message volume over time",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Messages per round",
    fill  = "Channel type"
  )










1.3.1 Side-Channel Use vs Main Channel
side_huddle and one_on_one_chat are outside Judge-Agent’s comms_huddle view. Their rise on breach day is directly observable.


Code
comms_tbl |>
  mutate(channel_group = case_when(
    channel == "comms_huddle"                                  ~ "comms_huddle (main)",
    channel %in% c("side_huddle", "one_on_one_chat")           ~ "side/1:1 (bypasses Judge)",
    channel %in% c("official_post","personal_post","anonymous_post") ~ "public post",
    TRUE ~ "other"
  )) |>
  count(round_hour, channel_group) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = round_hour, y = n, colour = channel_group, group = channel_group)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(ymd_hms("2046-06-05T00:00:00")),
             linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "4 days") +
  labs(
    title    = "Side-channel (side_huddle + one_on_one) messages vs main channel over time",
    subtitle = "side_huddle and one_on_one_chat are excluded from comms_huddle — Judge cannot see them",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Messages per round",
    colour   = "Channel group"
  )

text:
1.4 All Public Posts Timeline


Code
public_posts <- comms_tbl |>
  filter(is_public) |>
  mutate(
    is_breach_post = str_detect(
      str_to_lower(coalesce(content, "")),
      "definitive merger agreement|harborcrest residentedge|civicloom.*tenantthread.*merger|embargo formally lifted"
    )
  )

ggplot(public_posts, aes(x = timestamp, y = fct_rev(agent_label),
                          colour = channel, shape = is_breach_post)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(ymd_hms("2046-05-29T09:11:00")),
             linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text",
    x = ymd_hms("2046-05-29T09:11:00"), y = 7.2,
    label = "@Elena\nfaux pas", hjust = 0, size = 2.8, nudge_x = 3600*8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(ymd_hms("2046-06-05T17:17:00")),

  annotate("text",

title: Analysis
text:
1.6 Agent Activity on Breach Day
Who was speaking, on which channels, during the breach window (rounds 14–22)?


Code
comms_tbl |>
  filter(crisis_stage == "Breach window") |>
  count(agent_label, channel_type) |>
  mutate(agent_label = fct_reorder(agent_label, n, sum)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = agent_label, fill = channel_type)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            size = 3, colour = "white") +
  labs(
    title    = "Message counts by agent on breach day (Jun 5, rounds 14–22)",
    subtitle = "Internal = comms_huddle / side_huddle / one_on_one; Public = official / personal / anonymous",
    x        = "Message count",
    y        = NULL,
    fill     = "Channel type"
  )










1.6.1 Judge-Agent Activity Per Round
Was the compliance monitor present in each round?


Code
judge_per_round <- comms_tbl |>
  filter(agent_id == "judge_eval_agent") |>
  count(round_index, round_hour, name = "judge_msgs")

# Include all rounds (zero-fill where absent)
all_rounds <- comms_tbl |>
  distinct(round_index, round_hour, crisis_stage)

all_rounds |>
  left_join(judge_per_round, by = c("round_index","round_hour")) |>
  mutate(judge_msgs = replace_na(judge_msgs, 0L)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = round_hour, y = judge_msgs, fill = crisis_stage)) +
  geom_col(width = 3600 * 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(ymd_hms("2046-05-29T09:31:00")),
             linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text",
    x = ymd_hms("2046-05-29T12:00:00"), y = 9,
    label = "Judge\nassigned →", hjust = 0, size = 2.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(ymd_hms("2046-06-05T17:00:00")),
             linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text",
    x = ymd_hms("2046-06-05T14:00:00"), y = 9,
    label = "← 'Not\nobjecting'", hjust = 1, size = 2.8) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "4 days") +
  labs(
    title    = "Judge-Agent message count per round (0 = silent that round)",
    subtitle = "Breach-day side huddles where Legal orchestrated the release had zero Judge participation",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Messages",
    fill     = "Phase"
  )

1.7 Embargo Erosion: Severity Escalation Chart
Ten concrete events, each sourced from a message or environment_context, plotted to show how the embargo weakened over time.

erosion <- tribble(
  ~timestamp,              ~label,                                        ~severity,
  "2046-05-23 09:00",     "Interns start; no embargo briefing",          1,
  "2046-05-29 09:11",     "@Elena faux pas post (14 min live)",           2,
  "2046-05-29 09:31",     "Compliance monitor assigned (advisory only)",  2,
  "2046-06-04 09:00",     "SaltWind scoring exposé published",            3,
  "2046-06-05 10:20",     "Intern hears 'CivicLoom at 6 PM' in hallway", 3,
  "2046-06-05 11:34",     "Legal argues embargo 'functionally compromised'", 4,

title: Analysis
text:
3.1 Leading Indicators


Code
leading_daily <- leading_indicators |>
  mutate(day = as_date(timestamp)) |>
  summarise(
    `Sensitive language` = sum(warning_sensitive_language, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Side-channel use` = sum(warning_side_channel, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Public posts` = sum(warning_public_post, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Anonymous posts` = sum(warning_anonymous_post, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = day
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -day,
    names_to = "indicator",
    values_to = "count"
  )

ggplot(leading_daily, aes(x = day, y = count, fill = indicator)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "3 days") +
  labs(
    title = "Leading indicators before the embargo breach",
    subtitle = "Sensitive language, side-channel activity and public signals appeared before the final release",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of warning signals",
    fill = "Indicator"
  )

This table shows that Judge’s warning did not fully stop public signals. After the 3:08 PM warning, public posts continued before the 6:00 PM clearance. Some posts still carried deal-related, embargo-related or crisis-related signals, suggesting that Judge was not operating as a strict blocking control.
This shows the early release was not fully unexpected. The warning signs were there, but these signals did not trigger major action because they were still seen as manageable until Legal gave the 5:19 PM “GO”.

title: Analysis
text:
3.4 Interpretation
Yes, there were leading indicators that the early release was possible. Before the breach, the system already showed warning signs through sensitive language, side-channel coordination, public hints, and weak enforcement by Judge-Agent.
Earlier behaviours also differed from the expected. For example, the 29 May public/personal post created CivicLoom-related speculation before formal clearance.Later, sensitive information continued in side channels, Legal-Agent began reframing the embargo condition, and Judge-Agent did not impose a hard stop.
These incidents did not trigger noticeable action because each one looked manageable on its own. A public hint seemed like a small social media issue, side-channel discussion looked like crisis coordination, and Judge-Agent’s warning was treated as advice. Taken together, however, they show that the system was already fragile before the actual breach.

title: Tracing the Embargo Breach
text:
TenantThread’s merger announcement was supposed to remain under embargo until 6:00 PM on 5 June 2046. However, merger-related information appeared publicly on FleX before the official release time.
This project uses visual analytics to investigate how the breach happened, who was involved, how communication behaviour changed, and whether the release was a planned leak or a system breakdown under pressure.

title: Tracing the Embargo Breach
text:
Project Background
TenantThread is a property technology company involved in a sensitive merger with CivicLoom Realty Partners. The deal, codenamed Project HarborCrest, was under strict information embargo. At the same time, TenantThread was facing rising public pressure over its Retention Optimizer product and growing criticism from SaltWind Journal and social media users.
An automated compliance tool known as The Judge was introduced to prevent embargo breaches. However, during the crisis, embargoed merger information still appeared publicly before the official release time.
This project investigates the communication records from the two weeks leading up to the breach to understand what happened.

title: Tracing the Embargo Breach
text:
Investigation Focus
The central question of this project is:


Did TenantThread deliberately leak the merger, or did the system break down under pressure?


The analysis focuses on three areas:

Key events and relationships that led to the inappropriate release.
Behavioural changes between normal communication and crisis-period communication.
Leading indicators that showed the release was possible before it happened.

title: Tracing the Embargo Breach
text:
Analytical Approach
This project applies a structured visual analytics workflow to reconstruct the breach.





flowchart LR
  A[Raw MC1 JSON Data] --> B[Data Preparation]
  B --> C[Event Timeline]
  B --> D[Actor-Channel Analysis]
  B --> E[Sensitive Language Tracking]
  C --> F[Embargo Breach Sequence]
  D --> F
  E --> F
  F --> G[Leading Indicators]
  G --> H[Final Interpretation]






The analysis begins by transforming the nested MC1 JSON data into clean round-level and communication-level tables. These tables are then used to build visualisations that show how the breach developed over time.

title: Tracing the Embargo Breach
text:
Key Visual Analytics Components



Event Timeline
The timeline reconstructs the main sequence of events leading to the premature release. It highlights important triggers, decision points and public communication moments.


Actor-Channel Heatmap
The heatmap shows how actors used different channels across the crisis period. This helps reveal shifts from routine communication to side-channel and public-facing activity.



Sensitive Language Tracker
This view tracks deal-related, embargo-related and crisis-related terms over time. It helps identify when communication became more risky.


Leading Indicators View
This view identifies early warning signs, such as side-channel coordination, continued sensitive discussion after warnings, and public signalling before the official release.

title: Tracing the Embargo Breach
text:
Preliminary Finding
The preliminary finding is that the breach was not a planned leak by one individual from the start. Instead, it appears to be a system breakdown under pressure.
As the crisis intensified, TenantThread’s communication behaviour changed. The team moved from routine checking to urgent story control. After SaltWind’s 5:00 PM story, Legal treated the embargo as already overtaken by events and gave the “GO” at 5:19 PM. This led to merger-related posts being released before the official 6:00 PM embargo lift.

title: Tracing the Embargo Breach
text:
Expected Outcome
The expected outcome is an interactive visual analytics system that allows users to:

trace the full release pathway
compare normal and abnormal communication behaviour
identify the actors, channels and decisions involved
detect warning signs before the breach, and
assess whether the breach was deliberate or caused by system failure under pressure.

This project will combine timeline analysis, behavioural comparison and evidence-based interpretation to support CivicLoom’s legal investigation.

The analysis section examines the embargo breach, including communication patterns, Judge-Agent warnings, public posts and leading indicators.

text: This document walks through how we parse, clean, and reshape the raw VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1 dataset into the three relational tables, which are Rounds, Communications, and Participants.

title: Data Preparation
text:
1.1 Loading Packages
We use the following packages:

jsonlite - parse the JSON source file
tidyverse - data wrangling and string operations
lubridate - timestamp parsing
tidytext - tokenisation for keyword flagging and text analysis
knitr - formatted table output


pacman::p_load(jsonlite, tidyverse, lubridate, tidytext, knitr)

title: Data Preparation
text:
1.2 Loading Data
We load the single JSON file provided for VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1.

mc1_raw <- jsonlite::fromJSON("../data/MC1_final_00.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
rounds_raw <- mc1_raw$rounds
cat("Total rounds:", length(rounds_raw), "\n")

The dataset contains 23 rounds, spanning 17 May 2046 to 5 June 2046 (the day of the embargo breach). Each round holds an environment_context object, a flat list of communications, and a participants list recording each agent’s status for that round.

title: Data Preparation
text:
4.2 Cleaning corrupted stock prices






WarningKnown Data Quality Issues




event_headline for rounds 15 and 16 both read "10:00 AM.", corrected using the hour timestamp instead.
stock_price for several crisis-day rounds contains corrupted values ($180, NULL), replaced with prices quoted in agent messages.





Code
# Prices recovered from agent message content for each corrupt round
stock_price_fixes <- tribble(
  ~round_index, ~stock_price_clean,
  14L,  28.70,    # 09:00 — NULL, opening price from agent content
  15L,  31.50,    # 10:00 — NULL, interpolated from agent content
  16L,  NA_real_, # 11:00 — $180 corrupt, no reliable quote found
  19L,  26.90,    # 14:00 — $18.0 corrupt, use 13:00 price as reference
  20L,  32.80,    # 15:00 — $18.0 corrupt, quoted in side-huddle
  21L,  33.05,    # 16:00 — NULL, Sentinel 5:12 PM update
  22L,  33.05,    # 17:00 — NULL, same post-market reference
  23L,  33.05     # 18:00 — NULL, after-hours Sentinel final report
)

rounds_tbl <- rounds_tbl %>%
  select(-any_of(c("stock_price_raw_num", "is_corrupt",
                   "stock_price_clean", "pct_change_clean"))) %>%
  mutate(
    stock_price_raw_num = as.numeric(str_remove(stock_price_raw, "\\$")),
    is_corrupt = round_index %in% stock_price_fixes$round_index |
                 stock_price_raw_num %in% c(18, 18.0, 180) |
                 is.na(stock_price_raw)
  ) %>%
  left_join(stock_price_fixes, by = "round_index") %>%
  mutate(
    stock_price_clean = if_else(
      !is_corrupt,
      stock_price_raw_num,
      stock_price_clean
    ),
    pct_change_clean = as.numeric(str_remove(pct_change_raw, "%"))
  )

title: Data Preparation
text:
5.1 Extracting fields
We flatten all messages from all rounds into a single data frame. Internal state sub-fields (reacting, rationalizing, deliberating) are extracted as separate columns.


Code
comms_tbl <- map_dfr(seq_along(rounds_raw), function(i) {
  rnd  <- rounds_raw[[i]]
  hour <- ymd_hms(rnd$hour)

  map_dfr(rnd$communications, function(msg) {
    ist <- msg$internal_state %||% list()

    tibble(
      round_index    = i,
      round_hour     = hour,
      message_id     = msg$message_id     %||% NA_character_,
      agent_id       = msg$agent_id       %||% NA_character_,
      agent_role     = msg$agent_role     %||% NA_character_,
      agent_label    = msg$agent_label    %||% NA_character_,
      channel        = msg$channel        %||% NA_character_,
      message_type   = msg$message_type   %||% NA_character_,
      responding_to  = msg$responding_to  %||% NA_character_,
      content        = msg$content        %||% NA_character_,
      timestamp      = ymd_hms(msg$timestamp %||% NA_character_),
      recipients     = paste(unlist(msg$recipients %||% list()), collapse = ", "),
      # Internal state sub-fields
      st_reacting      = ist$reacting      %||% NA_character_,
      st_rationalizing = ist$rationalizing %||% NA_character_,
      st_deliberating  = ist$deliberating  %||% NA_character_
    )
  })
}) %>%
  left_join(crisis_stage_map, by = "round_index")

cat("Total messages:", nrow(comms_tbl), "\n")


Total messages: 912

title: Data Preparation
text:
5.2 Deriving temporal and structural columns


Code
comms_tbl <- comms_tbl %>%
  mutate(
    date              = as_date(timestamp),
    hour_of_day       = hour(timestamp),
    day_of_week       = wday(timestamp, label = TRUE),
    is_crisis_day     = date == as_date("2046-06-05"),
    # Minutes elapsed since first message in dataset (for continuous timeline)
    minutes_since_start = as.numeric(difftime(timestamp,
                                               min(timestamp, na.rm = TRUE),
                                               units = "mins")),
    # Channel groupings
    channel_type      = case_when(
      channel %in% c("comms_huddle", "side_huddle", "one_on_one_chat") ~ "Internal",
      channel %in% c("official_post", "personal_post", "anonymous_post") ~ "Public",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    is_side_channel   = channel %in% c("side_huddle", "one_on_one_chat"),
    is_public         = channel %in% c("official_post", "personal_post", "anonymous_post"),
    is_anonymous      = channel == "anonymous_post",
    is_broadcast      = recipients == "ALL",
    recipient_count   = if_else(
      is_broadcast,
      NA_integer_,
      str_count(recipients, ",") + 1L
    ),
    has_internal_state = !is.na(st_reacting) | !is.na(st_rationalizing) |
                         !is.na(st_deliberating)
  )

title: Data Preparation
text:
5.3 Keyword flagging
We create three Boolean flag columns on content and (where present) st_deliberating, covering deal-related, embargo-related, and crisis-related terms. A combined text field full_text is used for this scan.


Code
deal_terms    <- c("merger", "acquisition", "deal", "civicloom", "harborcrest",
                   "counterparty", "nda", "term sheet", "due diligence", "signing",
                   "strategic", "transaction", "partner")

embargo_terms <- c("embargo", "hold", "silence", "6 pm", "6:00", "release",
                   "clearance", "judge", "compliance", "unauthorized", "approved",
                   "restricted", "monitor")

crisis_terms  <- c("breach", "leak", "premature", "crisis", "firestorm",
                   "escalate", "saltwind", "oceancrunch", "ag inquiry",
                   "investigation", "viral", "senate", "attorney general")

flag_text <- function(text_col, terms) {
  pattern <- paste(terms, collapse = "|")
  str_detect(str_to_lower(text_col), pattern)
}

comms_tbl <- comms_tbl %>%
  mutate(
    full_text          = paste(coalesce(content, ""),
                                coalesce(st_deliberating, ""), sep = " "),
    flag_deal_terms    = flag_text(full_text, deal_terms),
    flag_embargo_terms = flag_text(full_text, embargo_terms),
    flag_crisis_terms  = flag_text(full_text, crisis_terms),
    flag_any           = flag_deal_terms | flag_embargo_terms | flag_crisis_terms
  )

DT::datatable(comms_tbl, caption = "Communications Table", options = list(pageLength = 5),class = "nowrap")

title: Data Preparation
text:
5.4 Back-filling comm_count into rounds table


Code
comm_counts <- comms_tbl %>%
  count(round_index, name = "comm_count")

rounds_tbl <- rounds_tbl %>%
  select(-any_of("comm_count")) %>%
  left_join(comm_counts, by = "round_index")

DT::datatable(rounds_tbl, caption = "Rounds Table", options = list(pageLength = 5),class = "nowrap")

title: Data Preparation
text:
6.1 Extracting fields
We extract one row per agent per round from the participants list, then parse declared_action into a clean action type and a separate content field.


Code
participants_tbl <- map_dfr(seq_along(rounds_raw), function(i) {
  rnd <- rounds_raw[[i]]
  map_dfr(rnd$participants %||% list(), function(p) {
    meta <- p$agent_round_metadata %||% list()
    tibble(
      round_index         = i,
      round_hour          = ymd_hms(rnd$hour),
      agent_id            = p$agent_id            %||% NA_character_,
      agent_role          = p$agent_role           %||% NA_character_,
      agent_label         = p$agent_label          %||% NA_character_,
      declared_action_raw = p$declared_action      %||% NA_character_,
      sentiment_at_turn   = meta$sentiment_at_turn %||% NA_character_,
      action_classification = meta$action_classification %||% NA_character_
    )
  })
}) %>%
  left_join(crisis_stage_map, by = "round_index")

title: Data Preparation
text:
6.2 Parsing declared action type
declared_action can be a short token (e.g. MONITORING) or a long string containing post content. We extract the action type prefix and store the remainder as action_content.


Code
participants_tbl <- participants_tbl %>%
  mutate(
    action_type = case_when(
      is.na(declared_action_raw)                            ~ NA_character_,
      str_starts(declared_action_raw, "MONITORING")         ~ "MONITORING",
      str_starts(declared_action_raw, "POSTED_ON_FLEX")     ~ "POSTED_ON_FLEX",
      str_starts(declared_action_raw, "POSTED_ANONYMOUS")   ~ "POSTED_ANONYMOUS",
      str_starts(declared_action_raw, "POSTED_PERSONAL")    ~ "POSTED_PERSONAL",
      str_starts(declared_action_raw, "COMPLIANCE_WARNING") ~ "COMPLIANCE_WARNING",
      TRUE                                                  ~ "OTHER"
    ),
    action_content = str_remove(declared_action_raw,
                                "^(MONITORING|POSTED_ON_FLEX|POSTED_ANONYMOUS|POSTED_PERSONAL|COMPLIANCE_WARNING)[:\\s—]*")
  )

DT::datatable(participants_tbl, options = list(pageLength = 5),class = "nowrap")

title: Data Preparation
text:
7.1 Expanding broadcast messages
Direct messages between agents.


Code
# Active agents per round (from participants table)
active_agents_per_round <- participants_tbl %>%
  select(round_index, agent_id) %>%
  distinct()

# Separate broadcast vs direct messages
direct_msgs <- comms_tbl %>%
  filter(!is_broadcast, !is.na(recipients), recipients != "") %>%
  separate_rows(recipients, sep = ",\\s*") %>%
  select(message_id, round_index, crisis_stage, timestamp, channel,
         sender = agent_id, recipient = recipients)

DT::datatable(direct_msgs, options = list(pageLength = 5),class = "nowrap")






Messages broadcasted among agents.


Code
broadcast_msgs <- comms_tbl %>%
  filter(is_broadcast) %>%
  select(message_id, round_index, crisis_stage, timestamp, channel,
         sender = agent_id) %>%
  left_join(active_agents_per_round, by = "round_index") %>%
  rename(recipient = agent_id) %>%
  filter(recipient != sender)

DT::datatable(broadcast_msgs, options = list(pageLength = 5),class = "nowrap")






Code
edges_tbl <- bind_rows(direct_msgs, broadcast_msgs) %>%
  # Remove messages with no identified recipient
  filter(!is.na(recipient), recipient != "") %>%
  # Exclude internal-state-only rows (no actual sender)
  filter(!is.na(sender))

cat("Total directed edges:", nrow(edges_tbl), "\n")


Total directed edges: 2003

text:
7.2 Adding edge weights by crisis stage

edges_weighted <- edges_tbl %>%
  group_by(sender, recipient, channel, crisis_stage) %>%
  summarise(
    weight         = n(),
    first_contact  = min(timestamp, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_contact   = max(timestamp, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups        = "drop"
  )

DT::datatable(edges_weighted, options = list(pageLength = 5),class = "nowrap")

title: Project Proposal
text: The project aims to understand how things can go wrong when people, systems, and tools have to work together under pressure. In VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1, TenantThread broke an embargo on its merger with CivicLoom Realty Partners when the news appeared early on FleX instead of the planned 6:00 PM release on 5 June 2046. This was not just a simple mistake of posting too early but a wider breakdown across Legal, PR, Social Media, Platform Trust, and an automated tool called “The Judge”, along with side channels and public accounts. The key question is whether this was a deliberate leak or a system failure. This project builds a visual analytics system to help reconstruct the sequence of events, compare normal and abnormal communication patterns, and identify early warning signs of the breach.

In VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1, TenantThread broke an embargo on its merger with CivicLoom Realty Partners when the news appeared early on FleX instead of the planned 6:00 PM release on 5 June 2046. This was not just a simple mistake of posting too early but a wider breakdown across Legal, PR, Social Media, Platform Trust, and an automated tool called “The Judge”, along with side channels and public accounts. The key question is whether this was a deliberate leak or a system failure. This project builds a visual analytics system to help reconstruct the sequence of events, compare normal and abnormal communication patterns, and identify early warning signs of the breach.

title: Project Proposal
text:
Objectives
This project aims to develop an interactive visual analytics tool to help analysts investigate the TenantThread embargo breach. The key objectives are:

Reconstruct the release sequence by showing the key events, actors, decisions, and links that led to the early release of merger information.
Compare normal and abnormal behaviour by analysing how communication changed from routine activity to crisis behaviour.
Identify actor and channel shifts by examining how different actors used official, internal, side, personal, and anonymous channels during the crisis.
Detect sensitive language patterns by tracking how deal-related, embargo-related and crisis-related language changed over time.
Assess the role of The Judge by examining whether it worked as a control tool or only as a warning system..
Detect early warning signs that could explain the breach and support legal analysis of whether it was a planned leak or a breakdown under pressure

title: Project Proposal
text:
Data
The project will use the data from VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1, which includes TenantThread’s internal and public communications before the embargo breach. The data will be organised into three tables:

Round-level table: one row per round or hour, with the timestamp, event headline, crisis stage, market information, social state, and communication count.
Communication-level table: one row per message, with the timestamp, actor role, actor label, channel, message type, content, and sensitive language flags.
Participants table: one row per participant, with the participant label, role, and channel usage.

The communications will be classified into four stages: pre-crisis, crisis before release, premature release, and post-embargo.

Known data quality issues:
Stock price fields in the market_snapshot for 5th June hourly rounds contain corrupted values ($18, $180). These will be replaced with prices quoted in agent messages for that period.

title: Project Proposal
text:
Methodology

Data Wrangling
Parse the JSON file and derive three relational tables, one for rounds, one for communications, and one for agents. Partition all 912 messages into four analytical windows: Pre-crisis, Crisis (pre-breach), Breach window, and Post-embargo.


Keyword flagging
Create flag columns, for example deal_terms, embargo_terms, crisis_terms.This is the foundational layer that identifies which messages are analytically relevant.


Temporal Analysis
To visualise how external pressure, internal communication patterns, and behavioural signals evolve over the 20-day period.

Market price across all 23 rounds, with communication volume.
The hourly communication volume and stock price on the crisis day.
Behavioural signal such as side-channel message volume, daily deal_term message count, and daily internal deliberation length.



Causal Analysis
Reconstruct the decision chain from the first structural failure to the breach, identifying the actors, the decisions, the causal mechanisms, and the gaps that prevented remediation at each step.

Reading of message content (internal state fields, which record agents’ private reasoning) with chronological ordering of events identified through temporal analysis and keyword flagging.
Each node in the causal chain includes the date and agent responsible, the event itself, the mechanism of which it enabled the next event.



Network Analysis
Construct communication network, using the ‘recipents’ field to define direct edges from sender to each recipients. Message frequency between agents will represent the edge weight.

Degree centrality: measures the number of distinct agents each node communicates with. A spike in out-degree for a particular agent in the breach window indicates that the agent expanded their communication reach during the crisis.
Betweenness centrality: identifies who is the gatekeeper, whose absence or non-compliance will cause systemic effects.
Eigenvector centrality: identifies agents who are connected to other influential agents.



Text Analysis
Perform sentiment analysis on the two layers of communication, which are the content field and deliberating field.
Keyness testing to identify which terms were statistically over-represented in the Breach and Crisis windows relative to the Pre-crisis baseline.

title: Project Proposal
text:
R Packages
The following R packages will be used to support data preparation, text analysis, timeline reconstruction, network analysis, behaviour comparison, and Shiny application development for Mini-Challenge 1.

Utility and Data Preparation

jsonlite: To import and parse the MC1 JSON dataset, which contains nested records such as rounds, environment context, communications, internal agent states, participants, and message metadata.
tidyverse: To clean, transform, filter, and summarize the dataset into analysis-ready tables.
dplyr: To group and compare communication records by agent, channel, message type, timestamp, and event period.
tidyr: To unnest nested JSON fields such as communications, internal states, media events, market snapshots, and agent metadata.
purrr: To handle repeated list-column operations when processing nested agent outputs and communications.
lubridate: To convert timestamps into proper date-time formats and support time-based filtering around the embargo breach.
stringr: To clean and extract keywords from message content, internal deliberations, public posts, hashtags, and references to Project HarborCrest or CivicLoom.
DT: To provide interactive tables for inspecting raw messages, filtered communications, and evidence linked to key events.



Text Analytics

tidytext: To tokenize messages and internal states for keyword frequency, phrase extraction, and comparison between normal communications and breach-related communications.
quanteda: To build document-feature matrices and compare language patterns across agents, channels, and time periods.
tm: To support text preprocessing such as corpus creation, stopword removal, and document-term matrix construction.
SnowballC: To apply stemming where useful, so related word forms can be grouped during text analysis.
sentimentr: To estimate sentiment and tone shifts in agent communications before and during the embargo breach.
widyr: To identify word correlations and co-occurring terms, such as links between Project HarborCrest, CivicLoom, embargo, The Judge, FleX, and announcement.



Timeline and Event Sequence Visualization

ggplot2: To create event timelines, agent activity charts, channel usage charts, and behaviour comparison plots.
plotly: To make timeline and activity visualizations interactive through hover labels, zooming, and filtering.
timevis: To create an interactive timeline showing the sequence of events leading up to the premature release.
ggrepel: To improve readability of annotated timeline labels, especially for key decision points and breach-related messages.



Network and Causal Relationship Analysis

igraph: To construct agent-to-agent and agent-to-system communication networks.
tidygraph: To manipulate network data using tidy data principles.
ggraph: To visualize relationships between agents, channels, decisions, public posts, and compliance checks.
visNetwork: To build an interactive network graph that allows users to explore who communicated with whom, through which channel, and around which key events.
networkD3: To create Sankey-style flow diagrams showing how information moved from internal deliberations to public FleX posts.
DiagrammeR: To create directed causal diagrams that explain the chain of decisions and system elements that allowed embargoed information to pass through enforcement.



Behaviour Comparison and Anomaly Detection

anomalize: To identify unusual changes in communication volume, channel usage, posting behaviour, or agent activity before the breach.
zoo: To calculate rolling averages and compare the breach period against prior baseline behaviour.
scales: To format dates, counts, and percentage changes clearly in visualizations.
forcats: To reorder categorical variables such as agents, channels, and message types based on frequency or importance.



Shiny Application Development

shiny: To build the main interactive visual analytics application.
bslib: To design a clean and modern dashboard interface.
shinyWidgets: To provide interactive filters such as agent selector, channel selector, date range selector, and message type selector.
shinycssloaders: To display loading indicators while large visualizations are being generated.
shinydashboard: To structure the application into sections such as overview, event timeline, network view, text analysis, anomaly detection, and evidence table.

These packages will support the development of a visual analytics system that helps users reconstruct the embargo breach, identify the key agents and decisions involved, compare breach behaviour against normal system behaviour, and detect earlier warning signs where agent behaviour differed from expected behaviour.
